agent_trace.summary: On a chest X-ray, the right hemidiaphragm should form a smooth, well-defined dome with the right lung base just above it and the liver providing a normal soft-tissue density beneath. An apparent abnormality by the right hemidiaphragm often reflects changes in the adjacent right lower lung, pleura, diaphragm contour, or upper abdominal structures, so side-specific localization is important. The retrieved SLAKE evidence is loosely relevant because it emphasizes laterality/location in chest X-ray questions, but it does not identify a specific diaphragmatic lesion.

key_facts: The right hemidiaphragm is normally slightly higher than the left due to the liver underneath.
A localized opacity near the right hemidiaphragm may represent right lower lobe air-space disease, pleural fluid, or subdiaphragmatic pathology.
Loss of the sharp right diaphragmatic contour can indicate adjacent lung base abnormality or pleural abnormality.
Free subdiaphragmatic air on X-ray is a critical abnormality, though it is usually seen under the diaphragm rather than just by it.
